sections.h2: Where Lake County property records are kept
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages and liens for Lake County go into the Official Records, which the clerk and comptroller maintains. The clerk's recording section handles deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, liens, powers of attorney, notices of commencement, agreements for deed, plats, judgments, financing statements and death certificates.

The clerk's website has a records search area, a guide to researching Official Records, a tax deed record search and a foreclosure sales calendar. The last two matter if a house has a delinquent history. The Property Appraiser keeps the parcel and ownership side, so a full picture of a house means checking both offices. The county has two clerk locations for in-person recording. Confirm their hours before you plan a closing day trip.

  • Clerk: recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens, tax deed files.
  • Property Appraiser: parcel data, owner of record on the tax roll, exemptions.
  • Tax Collector: tax bills and any certificate on the parcel.

Page one of a standard-size instrument costs $10.00, and each page after that is $8.50. Indexing adds $1.00 for every name over four.

The clerk's site also links a fee calculator for deeds and mortgages, worth running before you wire money to a closing agent.

sections.h2: What taxes does the clerk collect when a deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Documentary stamp tax on a deed is collected at recording. The rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction thereof, with a minimum of 70 cents on deeds whose consideration is $100 or less.

The tax follows every party to the document, and a deed owes it even if never recorded. An estate representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable, but quit claim deeds, contracts for deed and deeds in lieu are.

Mortgages carry two charges at recording: documentary stamps of 35 cents per $100 on the promise to pay, and a one-time intangible tax of 2 mills, which is .002 per $1. A cash sale with no new loan usually records just the deed, so ask the title company what is going on the record.

sections.h2: How to file a document in Lake County
sections.html:
Everything goes through the clerk's Recording Section, by one of four methods: in person, by mail, by drop box or by eRecording. Documents are recorded in the order received, typically within two business days. Same-day or next-day recording cannot be guaranteed for mail, drop box or electronic submissions.

If timing matters, record in person at one of the two locations. Make checks payable to the clerk and comptroller. Cashier's checks dated more than two months earlier are refused. Visa, MasterCard, Discover and American Express are taken, with a non-refundable processing fee on card payments.

  • Include an "this instrument prepared by" statement, which Florida law requires on the face of conveyances.
  • Use the clerk's Recording Transmittal Form to speed processing.
  • Leave out Social Security numbers unless the law requires them. If one slips in, the clerk will remove it from the online image on a written request, at no charge, which is a useful step for anyone who recorded paperwork years ago.
  • Expect the recorded document back by U.S. first class mail, with an envelope optional.

sections.h2: Can a Lake County owner watch for fraudulent deeds?
sections.html:
Yes. A free clerk service emails you when anything is recorded under a name you list, and each address can watch five names.

Scammers file false deeds to pose as owners and then collect money for rentals or sales. Owners of vacant, inherited or out-of-state houses are the most exposed, because nobody is watching the mailbox. Sign up through the clerk's recording notification service, and check the Official Records search yourself now and then for your surname.

Beyond the alert, keep your own address current with the Property Appraiser so tax notices reach you, and glance at the tax collector's record once a year for charges you do not recognize. Recording order matters too. Documents are recorded as received, so a deed and the mortgage that funds it should arrive together, and the closing agent usually sends them the same day.

sections.h2: Checking the records before you list
sections.html:
Pull the vesting deed and look for open mortgages, judgments, liens and a lis pendens, since each must be paid or released before a buyer gets clear title. A title company runs this search at closing, but running it first avoids surprises.

  • The deed names exactly who owns the house and how they hold title.
  • Any mortgage without a recorded satisfaction.
  • Notices of commencement or liens from contractors.
  • A lis pendens, which signals a lawsuit tied to the parcel.
  • Prior-year tax certificates, checked with the tax collector.

For an inherited house, ask the clerk's probate section what must be on file before the personal representative can sign a deed. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not on Florida's list of taxable deeds, a useful point to raise with your closing agent.

Print what you find and bring it, with a copy of your deed, to the first call with the title company. If a lien or old mortgage turns up, contact the holder for a release before you accept an offer. A cash buyer will still order a title search, so clearing items early protects your closing date.

sections.h2: How lis pendens and foreclosure show up in the records
sections.html:
A foreclosure suit appears in the Official Records as a lis pendens, priced at $5.00 for page one and $4.00 after. Releasing one costs $10.00 and $8.50.

State law puts the public sale between 20 and 35 days after a final judgment unless the plaintiff consents to longer. The sale notice runs two weeks in a row, and the winning bidder leaves a deposit. The clerk keeps a foreclosure sales calendar on its site, which is the place to confirm any sale date. A homeowner who sees a lis pendens against the house should talk to a Florida attorney, and can still sell before the sale if the payoff is covered.

faqs.q: Does the Lake County clerk record deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk acts as county recorder, so deeds, mortgages and liens all end up in the Official Records. Recording happens in the clerk's Recording Section.

faqs.q: What will a deed cost to file in Lake County?
faqs.a: Page one is $10.00 and later pages are $8.50 each, with $1.00 added per name past the fourth. Deed stamps are a separate charge.

faqs.q: How long does Lake County recording take?
faqs.a: Documents are recorded in order received, typically within two business days. Same-day recording is not guaranteed for mail, drop box or eRecording, so record in person if the date matters.

faqs.q: Can I record a Lake County document electronically?
faqs.a: Yes. eRecording is one of four ways to record, along with in person, mail and drop box.

faqs.q: Is there a free alert for new documents on my Lake County property?
faqs.a: Yes. A free email alert goes out when a document is recorded under a name you monitor, and five names fit on one address.
